title: Anuradhapura becomes the royal capital
dateNote: Chronicle chronology. Archaeology shows the city's main expansion and fortification in roughly the 4th-3rd centuries BCE.
summary: The Mahavamsa credits King Pandukabhaya with laying out Anuradhapura as a planned capital with gates, cemeteries, tanks and quarters for different communities. Excavations show the settlement growing into a fortified city with a rampart and moat.

evidence.description: Pandukabhaya's founding and layout of the city.
Urban growth and fortification phases at Salgaha Watta 2.

title: Mahinda's mission and royal adoption of Buddhism
summary: According to the chronicles, the monk Mahinda, son of the Mauryan emperor Asoka, met King Devanampiya Tissa at Mihintale and converted him. The Mahavihara monastery was then founded at Anuradhapura. Hundreds of cave inscriptions recording gifts of caves to the sangha appear from this period.

evidence.description: Mahinda's arrival on Missaka mountain and the conversion of the king.
Earlier account of the mission.
Asokan Rock Edicts II and XIII name Tambapamni among lands that received Asoka's dhamma and medical provisions.
Early Brahmi cave donations to the sangha at Mihintale and elsewhere.

historiography: The Asokan edicts confirm contact but do not mention Mahinda. The personal details of the mission come from later monastic chronicles. Buddhism may have arrived earlier and more gradually through trade.

title: Planting of the Sri Maha Bodhi
summary: The chronicles tell how the nun Sanghamitta brought a sapling of the Bodhi tree from Bodh Gaya, which was planted in the Mahamegha garden. The Sri Maha Bodhi at Anuradhapura is venerated as that tree.

evidence.description: Bringing and planting of the Bodhi sapling.
Faxian describes the Bodhi tree and its veneration in the early 5th century CE.

historiography: Faxian confirms the tree was being venerated by c. 410 CE. There is no independent evidence for the 3rd-century BCE date, but the chronicles present it as continuous.

title: Early Brahmi cave inscriptions across the island
summary: More than a thousand short Prakrit inscriptions in early Brahmi script record gifts of rock-shelter dwellings to Buddhist monks. They name donors including chiefs (parumaka), householders, merchants and royalty, and are a key source for social structure.

evidence.description: Corpus edition and translation of the early Brahmi inscriptions.

historiography: Paranavitana's readings are foundational but some have been revised. A few inscriptions name individuals with Tamil associations, which bears on early ethnic history (see Indrapala 2005).

title: Urban centre at Tissamaharama (Ruhuna)
summary: Excavations at Akurugoda in Tissamaharama reveal a major early historic town in the southern region of Ruhuna, with workshops, coins and imported goods. The chronicles describe Mahagama as the seat of a southern dynasty.

evidence.description: Sri Lankan-German excavations of the early town.
Mahagama as a seat of rulers in Ruhuna.

title: Dutthagamani defeats Elara
summary: The Mahavamsa's longest narrative tells how Dutthagamani of Ruhuna fought a campaign north against Elara, a Chola-origin king who had ruled Anuradhapura for many years. He killed Elara in single combat, unified the island under one ruler, and then built great Buddhist monuments.

evidence.description: Elara's reign and the campaign of Dutthagamani.

historiography: The account was written centuries later with strong religious framing. The chronicle itself calls Elara a just ruler. In the 20th century the episode became a powerful and contested symbol in nationalist discourse.

perspectives.label: Chronicle framing
perspectives.view: A war to restore the Buddhist dispensation; the chronicle also records that Dutthagamani honoured Elara's tomb.

perspectives.label: Modern scholarship
perspectives.view: The episode reflects competition between regional elites and was later reworked as an ethnic narrative.

title: Construction of the Mahathupa (Ruwanwelisaya)
summary: The chronicles credit Dutthagamani with starting the Great Stupa, completed by his brother Saddhatissa. It remains one of the defining monuments of the Anuradhapura sacred city, which UNESCO inscribed in 1982.

evidence.description: Detailed account of the construction and enshrinement.
Standing monument (heavily restored in the 20th century).
Sacred City of Anuradhapura, World Heritage inscription 1982.

title: Pali Canon committed to writing at Aluvihare
summary: During the reign of Vattagamani Abhaya, after a period of famine and invasion, monks wrote down the Tipitaka and its commentaries, which until then had been passed on orally. Tradition places this at Aluvihare near Matale.

evidence.description: Writing down of the canon in the reign of Vattagamani.
Parallel account.

historiography: The writing-down is widely accepted. The specific location at Aluvihare comes from later tradition rather than the earliest chronicles.

title: Embassy from Taprobane to Emperor Claudius
summary: Pliny the Elder records that a freedman of Annius Plocamus was blown off course to Taprobane. The king then sent an embassy of four envoys to Rome, and Pliny reports their descriptions of the island.

evidence.description: Pliny's account of Taprobane and the embassy.

historiography: This is the fullest classical description of the island, though it mixes reliable report with marvel literature. Roman coins found widely in Sri Lanka (mostly late Roman) show later trade connections.

title: Mantai: Indian Ocean port city
dateLabel: c. 2nd century BCE - c. 11th century CE
summary: Mantai (Mahatittha), opposite the Indian coast near Mannar, was the island's chief port for long-distance trade. Excavations recovered Chinese ceramics, Islamic glazed wares, Mediterranean and Persian material, and evidence of bead and gem working.

evidence.description: Final report on the 1980-84 excavations.
Cosmas describes Sielediba as a hub between China and the West in the 6th century.

title: Mahasena builds the Jetavana and great tanks
summary: King Mahasena backed the Abhayagiri faction against the Mahavihara and built the Jetavana stupa, at the time among the tallest structures in the world. He is also credited with major reservoirs, including Minneriya.

evidence.description: Mahasena's reign and conflict with the Mahavihara.
Jetavana stupa; analysis of monastic architecture.
Economic role of monasteries and irrigation.

historiography: The Mahavamsa was written from the Mahavihara's point of view, so its portrayal of Mahasena is partisan.

title: The Tooth Relic arrives from Kalinga
summary: The Culavamsa records that the Buddha's tooth relic was brought from Kalinga in the reign of Sirimeghavanna. The relic became the palladium of Sri Lankan kingship and moved with the capital through the centuries, finally to Kandy.

evidence.description: Arrival of the tooth relic.
Faxian describes the annual tooth-relic festival at Anuradhapura c. 410 CE.

wiki: Relic of the tooth of the Buddha

title: Chinese pilgrim Faxian in Lanka
summary: The monk Faxian spent about two years at Anuradhapura collecting Vinaya texts. He described the Abhayagiri monastery with 5,000 monks, the Mahavihara with 3,000, the jade Buddha image and merchants from many lands, and his account is an independent check on the chronicles.

evidence.description: Faxian's account of Simhala.

title: Buddhaghosa and the Pali commentaries
summary: The Indian scholar-monk Buddhaghosa worked at the Mahavihara, composing the Visuddhimagga and translating the Sinhala commentaries into Pali. This work shaped Theravada orthodoxy across South and Southeast Asia.

evidence.description: Buddhaghosa's arrival and work.

title: Dhatusena builds Kala Wewa
summary: King Dhatusena expelled South Indian rulers and built the great Kala Wewa reservoir, linked to Anuradhapura by the gently graded Jaya Ganga (Yoda Ela) canal, an outstanding example of ancient hydraulic engineering.

evidence.description: Dhatusena's reign and works.
Irrigation economy and monastic landholding.

title: Kassapa I's palace-fortress at Sigiriya
summary: After deposing his father Dhatusena, Kassapa I moved the capital to Sihagiri, a rock with palace, water gardens, frescoes and a lion gateway. Visitors' verses scratched on the Mirror Wall from the 8th to 10th centuries are an important source for early Sinhala.

evidence.description: Kassapa's parricide and the building of Sihagiri.
The Mirror Wall graffiti.
Ancient City of Sigiriya, World Heritage inscription 1982.

historiography: Paranavitana later argued, citing 'interlinear inscriptions' that only he could read, that Sigiriya was designed as the abode of the god Kuvera. Most epigraphers reject these readings. The site also had an earlier and later life as a Buddhist monastery.

title: Cosmas describes Sielediba as an entrepot
summary: The Christian Topography of Cosmas Indicopleustes describes the island as a meeting point for ships from China and from Persia and the Red Sea. It notes a Persian Christian church on the island and an audience at court between Roman and Persian merchants.

evidence.description: Description of Taprobane/Sielediba.
Material evidence for long-distance trade at Mantai.

title: Chola conquest and the end of Anuradhapura
summary: Rajaraja I of the Chola empire invaded the north around 993, and Rajendra I completed the conquest in 1017, capturing King Mahinda V and taking him to India. Anuradhapura was sacked, and the Cholas ruled Rajarata from Polonnaruwa, renamed Jananathamangalam, where Hindu temples were built.

evidence.description: Chola invasion and the capture of Mahinda V.
Chola royal inscriptions and Tamil inscriptions in Sri Lanka, analysed for the politics of the conquest.
Chola-period Siva devales at Polonnaruwa.

title: The chronology problem of the early kings
summary: The chronicles count dates from the Buddha's death, traditionally placed in 544 BCE. That would make Devanampiya Tissa (accession 307 BCE) too early to be a contemporary of Asoka (c. 268-232 BCE). Geiger therefore re-based the chronology on c. 483 BCE, shifting early reigns about 60 years later.

evidence.description: Regnal years as given in the chronicle.
Asokan edicts used to anchor the synchronism.
Discussion of alternative chronologies.

historiography: This atlas stores rulers in the conventional chronology and gives Geiger's dates where they differ. Events dated through the Asokan synchronism (Mahinda's mission, the Bodhi tree) are placed c. 250 BCE. Expect apparent mismatches of about 60 years before the 2nd century CE.

title: Thuparama: the first stupa
summary: The chronicle says relics, including the right collarbone of the Buddha, were enshrined in the Thuparama, the island's first stupa.

evidence.description: The arrival of the relics.
Stupa and vatadage remains.

title: Founding of Abhayagiri Vihara
summary: Vattagamani Abhaya founded Abhayagiri after regaining his throne. It became the great rival of the Mahavihara, open to Mahayana teachings, and an international centre. Faxian found 5,000 monks there.

evidence.description: Founding of Abhayagiri.
Description of Abhayagiri c. 410 CE.
Monastic economy and sectarian rivalry.

title: Godavaya: early port and shipwreck
summary: Divers found a cargo wreck off Godavaya carrying glass ingots, iron and stone querns, possibly the oldest known shipwreck in South Asian waters. On land, a rock inscription attributed to Gajabahu I grants the harbour's customs revenue to a monastery.

evidence.description: Underwater survey and analysis of the assemblage.
Godavaya inscription of the reign of Gajabahu I.

historiography: The wreck's date rests on a limited number of radiocarbon samples.

title: Roman and local coinage in circulation
summary: Late Roman bronze coins and local imitations are found in large numbers across Sri Lanka, alongside earlier punch-marked coins and local 'Lakshmi plaque' issues. They show the island's place in Indian Ocean exchange.

evidence.description: Catalogue and analysis of coins from Tissamaharama and elsewhere.
Cosmas's story of the Roman and Persian coins at the Sinhala court.

title: Wind-powered iron smelting at Samanalawewa
summary: Survey of the southern escarpment found dozens of furnace sites positioned to catch the monsoon winds. Experimental reconstruction showed they could produce high-carbon steel, making Sri Lanka a candidate source of the famed 'Serendib' steel.

evidence.description: Field survey, excavation and experimental smelting.
Full monograph.

title: The Avukana Buddha
summary: A colossal rock-cut standing Buddha about 12 m tall. Tradition attributes it to Dhatusena, but art historians date it to between the 5th and 9th centuries on stylistic grounds.

evidence.description: Stylistic analysis of the image.

historiography: The traditional attribution comes from its closeness to Dhatusena's Kala Wewa, not from an inscription.

title: Dambulla cave temple
summary: A rock-shelter monastery with early Brahmi donative inscriptions grew into the island's largest cave temple. Kirti Sri Rajasinha had its interiors repainted in the 18th century.

evidence.description: Early Brahmi inscriptions at the site.
World Heritage inscription 1991.

title: Manavamma takes the throne with Pallava help
summary: Manavamma, an exiled prince, served the Pallava king Narasimhavarman I and returned with a Pallava army to win the throne. The episode marks close ties with the Pallava court, visible in art and architecture.

evidence.description: Manavamma's exile and return.

title: Pandyan sack of Anuradhapura and reprisal
summary: Under Sena I the Pandyan king Srimara Srivallabha invaded and plundered Anuradhapura. Sena II then sent an army that sacked Madurai and placed a Pandyan prince on the throne.

evidence.description: Invasion under Sena I and counter-invasion under Sena II.
South Indian context.

title: Badulla pillar inscription: regulating a market
summary: A long inscribed pillar sets out royal regulations for the market town of Hopitigama: fair weights, tolls and the punishment of crimes. It is rare direct evidence for trade and local administration.

evidence.description: Text and translation of the pillar inscription.

review.notes: Add the volume and page for the Epigraphia Zeylanica edition.

title: Early Muslim traders and the Colombo Kufic inscription
summary: Arab and Persian merchants were active in the island's ports from the late first millennium. A Kufic tombstone found in Colombo, dated to the mid-10th century, is among the earliest Islamic inscriptions in Sri Lanka.

evidence.description: History of Muslim settlement.
Arab geographers and Cosmas on earlier trade.

review.notes: Verify the inscription date and edition.

title: Early coinage: punch-marked coins and Lakshmi plaques
summary: The earliest money on the island includes punch-marked silver coins (kahapana) and locally cast 'Lakshmi plaques' showing a goddess standing on a lotus, found in early historic levels.

evidence.description: Coins from the Tissamaharama excavations.
Classic survey of Ceylon coinage.

title: Founding of the bhikkhuni order
summary: The chronicles say Queen Anula and her women were ordained by Sanghamitta, founding the order of nuns. Sri Lankan nuns took the ordination lineage to China in 433 CE. The order seems to have died out in the turmoil of the 11th century.

evidence.description: Ordination of Anula and the coming of Sanghamitta.
History of Buddhist women renunciants in Sri Lanka.

historiography: The transmission of the lineage to China is recorded in Chinese sources and is central to modern debates over reviving the order.
